section.title: Sing to the Lord a New Song
section.sectionRationale: A hymn of praise celebrating the LORD's upright word, His creative power in speaking the heavens into being, and His sovereign counsel that stands forever above every plan of nations and kings, closing with a plea that His loving devotion would rest on those who wait for Him.
section.thesis: The same LORD whose word spoke the heavens into existence and whose counsel stands forever above every human plan is the God whose eyes rest on those who fear Him and hope in His loving devotion.
section.frameNote: Five movements: a call to sing a new song of praise (1-3); the upright word of the LORD and His creative power (4-9); the LORD's counsel standing forever above the plans of nations (10-12); His watchful care over all humanity and the futility of trusting in military strength (13-17); and His eyes on those who fear Him, closing in a prayer that His loving devotion would rest upon them (18-22).

units.label: Sing to Him a new song

verses.text: Rejoice in the LORD, O righteous ones; it is fitting for the upright to praise Him.
Praise the LORD with the harp; make music to Him with ten strings.
Sing to Him a {{chadash|new}} song; play skillfully with a shout of joy.

units.label: By the word of the LORD the heavens were made
units.note: the upright word and creative power of God

verses.text: For the word of the LORD is upright, and all His work is trustworthy.
The LORD loves righteousness and justice; the earth is full of His loving devotion.
By the {{dabar|word}} of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth.
He piles up the waters of the sea; He puts the depths into storehouses.
Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the people of the world revere Him.
For He spoke, and it came to be; He commanded, and it stood firm.

units.label: The counsel of the LORD stands forever

verses.text: The LORD frustrates the plans of the nations; He thwarts the devices of the peoples.
The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the purposes of His heart to all generations.
Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people He has chosen as His inheritance!

units.label: He shapes the hearts of each
units.note: watchful care and the futility of human strength

verses.text: The LORD looks down from heaven; He sees all the sons of men.
From His dwelling place He gazes on all who inhabit the earth.
He shapes the hearts of each; He considers all their works.
No king is saved by his vast army; no warrior is delivered by his great strength.
A horse is a vain hope for salvation; even its great strength cannot save.

units.label: May Your loving devotion rest on us
units.note: eyes of the LORD and closing prayer

verses.text: Surely the eyes of the LORD are on those who fear Him, on those whose hope is in His {{chesed|loving devotion}}
to deliver them from death and keep them alive in famine.
Our soul waits for the LORD; He is our help and our shield.
For our hearts rejoice in Him, since we trust in His holy name.
May Your loving devotion rest on us, O LORD, as we put our hope in You.

chadash.gloss: New, fresh. A new song does not discard old songs but responds afresh to a fresh sight of God's works, an ongoing theme across the Psalter, later echoed in Revelation's new song sung before the Lamb, Revelation 5:9.

dabar.gloss: Word, speech, matter. The LORD's dabar spoke the heavens into being, the same creative Word John identifies as eternally with God and as God, through whom all things were made, John 1:1-3.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion. The psalm both opens, verse 5, and closes, verse 22, on this quality of God, filling the earth and resting specifically on those who hope in Him.

basic.context: The psalm calls the righteous to sing a new song of praise, grounding that praise in the LORD's upright word and trustworthy work, most dramatically displayed in creation, where the heavens were made by His word and the stars by the breath of His mouth. It then turns to God's sovereignty over history, His counsel standing forever above the plans of nations, and to His watchful care over every human heart, contrasting the futility of trusting in armies and horses with the security of those who fear the LORD. It closes with a prayer that God's loving devotion would rest on those who hope in Him.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm should be read as worship that moves naturally from creation to providence to personal hope, teaching that the same power that spoke galaxies into being is the power sustaining and directing history and personal lives, so that trust in God, not human strength, is the only sure foundation.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm calls for a chadash, new, song, responding freshly to God's works, celebrates His dabar, word, by which the heavens were made, and closes appealing to His chesed, steadfast covenant loving devotion, both filling the whole earth and resting specifically on those who hope in Him.
basic.typology: The LORD's word by which the heavens were made, verses 6 and 9, anticipates the eternal Word identified in John 1:1-3 as with God and as God, through whom all things were made, and by whom all things continue to be sustained and hold together, Colossians 1:16-17.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Word, the dabar, by which the heavens were made, John 1:1-3, the same creative power this psalm celebrates now revealed as a person, through whom and for whom all things exist and in whom all things hold together, Colossians 1:16-17. Where the psalm declares that no king is saved by a vast army and no warrior by great strength, verse 16, Christ's kingdom is established not by earthly force but by His death and resurrection, and His counsel, unlike any earthly ruler's, truly stands forever, fulfilling verse 11 completely, Hebrews 13:8.
basic.god: God is shown as sovereign over both creation and history, His word alone sufficient to bring galaxies into being and His counsel alone able to stand firm despite every scheme of nations, while remaining intimately attentive to the hearts of every individual person He has made.
basic.crossReferences: John 1:1-3 identifies Jesus as the eternal Word through whom all things were made, fulfilling this psalm's picture of creation by God's spoken word. Colossians 1:16-17 shows Christ sustaining all created things, the ongoing fulfillment of the LORD's word holding creation firm, verse 9. Hebrews 13:8 declares Jesus Christ the same yesterday, today, and forever, the New Testament's confirmation that His counsel, unlike human plans, truly stands to all generations.
basic.oneStory: The LORD whose word spoke the heavens into being and whose counsel stands forever above every human plan reveals Himself fully in Jesus Christ, the eternal Word through whom all things were made and by whom all things are sustained, in whom God's steadfast loving devotion finally and completely rests upon all who hope in Him.

context.literary:
This psalm has twenty two verses, the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, though it is not an acrostic. Many readers take the count as a quiet sign of completeness, praise from A to Z. Whether or not that was intended, the poem is carefully built, and its parts balance one another.

It opens with a summons in verses 1 to 3, a run of commands to rejoice, praise, sing, play and shout, addressed to the righteous. Verses 4 to 9 give the first reason, introduced by 'for': the word and work of the LORD, culminating in creation. Verses 10 to 19 give the second, and they move from the nations to the individual. Verses 20 to 22 are the response of the congregation, spoken as 'we' and 'us', and they close the frame by returning to rejoicing and to the LORD's loving devotion.

The heart of the poem is the pair of verses on the counsel of God, verses 10 and 11. The plans of the nations are frustrated, and the plans of the LORD stand. The two sentences share a key noun: the 'devices' of the peoples in verse 10 and the 'purposes' of His heart in verse 11 are the same word in Hebrew, so that the poem sets human planning and divine planning side by side and lets the reader see which one lasts.

A second balance concerns the gaze of God. In verses 13 to 15 the LORD looks down from heaven at all the sons of men and shapes and considers their hearts. In verse 18 His eyes fall on those who fear Him. The same eyes, first universal and then particular, move from the many to the few. The psalm's sense of scale is enormous, stretching from the stars in verse 6 to the human heart in verse 15, and the effect is that the God who made the vault of heaven is also the one who knows each person.

The psalm also turns on the word 'word' in one form or another: the word of the LORD in verse 4 and verse 6, and 'He spoke' and 'He commanded' in verse 9. Speech, creation and history are all pictured as the expression of a single will.
context.historical:
The psalm has no heading in the Hebrew text, which is unusual in this part of the Psalter, and the Greek version of the psalms attributes it to David. Its setting is the public worship of Israel, with the instruments named in verse 2. The harp and the ten stringed lyre were the ordinary tools of temple praise, and the call to play skillfully and with a shout of joy shows that music in worship was meant to be well done. The word for a shout, terua, is used of the blast of trumpets and the cry of a people at the presence of their king.

The middle of the psalm reflects the political world of the ancient Near East. Kings and their armies dominated it, and the horse was the ultimate weapon, in the form of chariot teams. Israel was warned against relying on it. The law told the king not to multiply horses for himself, Deuteronomy 17:16, and the prophets rebuked those who went to Egypt for help and relied on horses, Isaiah 31:1. The psalm's declaration that a horse is a vain hope, verse 17, is a distillation of that Israelite instinct, and it would have been sung by a people surrounded by empires far more powerful than themselves.

The picture in verse 7 of the waters piled up as in a heap draws on the memory of the exodus. The verb for piling is used at the Red Sea, where the waters 'piled up' at the blast of God's nostrils, Exodus 15:8, and again at the crossing of the Jordan, Joshua 3:13-16. The psalm blends the story of creation with the story of redemption: the God who set the limits of the sea also divided it for His people.

The phrase 'the nation whose God is the LORD' in verse 12 belongs to the covenant identity of Israel, a people that God chose as His inheritance, Deuteronomy 32:8-9. The hearers would also have recognised the mention of famine in verse 19 as a real danger in a land that depended on rain. To be kept alive in famine was to receive, from God, what the harvest could not guarantee.
context.canonical:
The psalm is a companion to the psalm before it. Psalm 32 ends with a call to the righteous to be glad in the LORD and rejoice, and Psalm 33 begins with the same call, 'Rejoice in the LORD, O righteous ones'. The phrase 'loving devotion', chesed, links the two as well, Psalm 32:10 and Psalm 33:5, 33:18 and 33:22. The forgiven man of one psalm becomes the singing congregation of the next.

The call to 'sing a new song' is a refrain of the Psalter and the prophets. It occurs in Psalm 40:3, Psalm 96:1, Psalm 98:1 and Isaiah 42:10, and each time it follows a fresh act of God. The last books of the Bible take it up again: the living creatures and elders sing a new song to the Lamb who was slain, Revelation 5:9, and the redeemed sing it before the throne, Revelation 14:3.

The account of creation by the word of the LORD in verses 6 and 9 is the psalm's central theological claim, and it rests on the opening chapter of Genesis, where 'God said, "Let there be light," and there was light', Genesis 1:3. The theme continues in Psalm 148:5, 'He gave the command and they were created', and in the New Testament. Hebrews 11:3 says 'the universe was formed at God's command'. Peter speaks of the heavens existing 'by God's word', 2 Peter 3:5. And John opens his Gospel with the Word through whom all things were made, John 1:1-3.

The teaching on human plans is at home in wisdom literature: 'Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail', Proverbs 19:21, and 'A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD', Proverbs 21:31. The prophets share the doctrine, and God says in Isaiah 46:10, 'My purpose will stand.' The theme of the chosen people as God's inheritance is echoed in 1 Peter 2:9-10, where the church is called a chosen people and a holy nation.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist meant to convince his hearers that praise is the fitting response to what is true about the world, and not merely a pleasant duty. Verse 1 says that praise is 'fitting' for the upright, and the rest of the poem gives the reasons. The word of the LORD is upright, His works are trustworthy, He loves justice, the earth is full of His covenant love, and He made everything by speaking. The hearer is invited to sing with his eyes open.

He also meant to loosen the grip of the world's power on the imagination. Israel lived among armies and empires, and every nation's plans seemed to determine the future. The poem reduces these plans to the status of a human sketch that God can frustrate, and it places the true plan in a heart that does not change, verse 11. A hearer who took this in would be freed from panic at the news of a stronger neighbour.

The poem is also meant to steer the people towards a particular kind of trust. It does not deny that armies and horses exist, and it does not say that they are of no use. It says they cannot save. The safety of a king or warrior depends on the one who watches. The closing prayer, that God's loving devotion may rest on those who hope, tells the people what their posture should be: waiting, not scheming, and trusting the LORD's name, verses 20 to 22.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes what God is like and what He has done, and on that basis it commands worship and trust. The commands are plain: rejoice, praise, sing, fear the LORD, verses 1 to 3 and 8. The statements about God are descriptions of His character and works, and the psalm does not tell us to imitate the creating word, or to consider ourselves free from all earthly means.

Verses 16 and 17 need care. The psalm says that no king is saved by a big army and no horse can save, but it does not command a nation to disband its defences or forbid the use of ordinary means. Elsewhere, Scripture treats planning and preparation as wise, as Proverbs 21:31 does in the same breath as it says the victory belongs to the LORD. The psalm's point is about where ultimate trust lies. The verse about famine in verse 19 is likewise a statement about God's care, not a promise that no believer will ever die of hunger. It is a truth to be held in faith, and it is not a formula for guaranteeing outcomes.

debates.question: Does 'the word of the LORD' and 'the breath of His mouth' in verse 6 point to the Son and the Spirit?

views.label: A hint of the Trinity
views.case: The verse puts word and breath together in the making of the heavens, and the Hebrew word for breath is the same as the word for spirit, ruach. Since Genesis 1:2 speaks of the Spirit of God hovering over the waters and 1:3 of God speaking, and since John 1:1-3 says all things were made through the Word, many Christian readers have heard the Son and the Spirit here. Some of the church fathers spoke of the Son and the Spirit as the two hands of God in creation.

views.label: Poetic parallelism for God's effortless command
views.case: Word and breath are two ways of saying one thing in parallel lines, and the 'breath of His mouth' is what speech is made of. On this reading the verse says that God made the heavens by simply speaking, with no labour, and it does not distinguish divine persons.

views.label: A true echo, seen in the light of later revelation
views.case: The psalmist meant to say that God creates by speaking, and the New Testament shows more than he saw. The later revelation does not contradict the original meaning. It shows that the God who spoke did so through His Word and by His Spirit.

debates.bearing: The third view respects both the original sense and the later revelation. The psalm makes no claim about persons on its own, but the way the New Testament speaks of creation through the Word and by the Spirit fits it naturally, and the church has rightly seen it as a witness.

debates.question: Who is 'the nation whose God is the LORD' in verse 12?

views.label: Israel alone
views.case: The description 'the people He has chosen as His inheritance' recalls the language of Deuteronomy 32:8-9, where the LORD's portion is His people. On this view the verse is a statement of Israel's unique covenant standing and its blessing.

views.label: Any nation that honours the LORD
views.case: The verse is a general beatitude, and it has been applied to any nation that acknowledges God. Proverbs 14:34 says that righteousness exalts a nation. Some treat the verse as a principle for public life.

views.label: The church, the people of God from every nation
views.case: Peter takes up the language of a chosen people and holy nation and applies it to the church, 1 Peter 2:9-10. On this reading the verse is fulfilled in a people drawn from all nations, and the blessing is given to them in Christ.

debates.bearing: The verse belongs first to Israel, and it is not a licence to treat any modern state as God's chosen nation. The New Testament gathers the people of God from every nation, and the verse rests on the covenant God makes with those who belong to Him.

debates.question: How far does 'the counsel of the LORD stands forever' reach over human plans?

views.label: God's purposes govern every detail
views.case: Verses 10 and 11 contrast human plans, which are frustrated, with the LORD's counsel, which stands. Isaiah 46:10 and Ephesians 1:11 speak of God working out everything according to the counsel of His will. On this reading nothing escapes His governing purpose.

views.label: God's broad purposes stand, while human freedom is real
views.case: The psalm speaks of the ultimate outcome of history and of the failure of schemes that oppose God, without saying how each decision is determined. Human plans are real, and they may succeed for a time, but they cannot overturn God's aims.

debates.bearing: Both views hold that no human plan can finally defeat God's purpose. They differ on how God's rule relates to human choice, which the psalm does not address. The practical point is the same: those who trust Him need not fear that the plans of the powerful will have the last word.

study.originalLanguages:
The command 'Sing to Him a new song' has the noun shir chadash, and it is more than a call to compose something novel. Each occurrence in the Psalter and Isaiah follows an act of God that deserves fresh words, as in Psalm 40:3 and Isaiah 42:10. The next phrase, 'play skillfully with a shout of joy', joins two ideas. The verb of skill means to do something well, and the noun for a shout, teruah, is the sound of trumpet and acclamation. Worship is to be both artful and loud.

In verse 4 the word of the LORD is 'upright', yashar, meaning straight or level, the opposite of crooked. His work is 'trustworthy', from the root of amen and emunah, meaning firm and reliable. The two adjectives set the words and works of God side by side as things that can bear weight. Verse 5 says the earth is full of His chesed. A phrase like that is used of God's glory in Isaiah 6:3, and Psalm 119:64 uses the same wording for His loving devotion. The whole world is a vessel filled with His covenant love.

The centre of the creation section is verse 6, and the Greek Old Testament renders its two parts with 'word', logos, and 'spirit', pneuma. The Hebrew 'breath of His mouth' uses ruach, so that the translators saw spirit and word working together, and John's Gospel takes up logos to name the Son. The 'stars' are literally the host, tsava, the same word used elsewhere of armies and of the angelic court, so that the sky is pictured as a host mustered by a word.

Verse 7 says that God 'piles up' the waters, from the noun ned, a heap or mound. The word is used for the walls of water at the Red Sea in Exodus 15:8 and at the Jordan in Joshua 3:13. The 'depths' are put into storehouses, a picture of order: the abyss is stored like grain. The pairing of creation with exodus vocabulary is intentional.

Verses 10 and 11 turn on one noun. The 'devices' of the peoples and the 'purposes' of God's heart are both machashavot, plans or thoughts. The verbs for what God does with human plans are strong: He 'frustrates', from the root that means to break or annul, and 'thwarts', another strong verb of hindering. Against these, God's counsel 'stands', from the verb amad, the same verb used in verse 9 of creation that 'stood firm'. What God speaks stands, and what He plans stands.

In verse 15 the BSB says 'He shapes the hearts of each'. The Hebrew for the shaper is the word for a potter, the participle of yatsar, as in Genesis 2:7, and the word rendered 'of each' is yachad, which usually means 'together' or 'alike'. Some translations say He 'fashions their hearts all alike', or 'together'. The choice affects whether the verse speaks of individuals or of the common human make up. Verse 17 calls the horse a 'vain hope', literally a lie, sheqer, meaning that it deceives those who trust it.

The closing verses turn to waiting. 'Our soul waits' comes from a verb of patient expectation, and the 'hope' in verses 18 and 22 is yachal, a word that also closes Psalm 31, in verse 24. The last verse asks that God's chesed should be upon the worshippers 'as' they hope, a comparison that makes the hope the measure of the mercy they ask for.

typology.fulfillment: The LORD made the heavens by His word, and the New Testament identifies the agent of that word. 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... Through Him all things were made', John 1:1-3. Paul says, 'all things were created through Him and for Him', Colossians 1:16, and Hebrews says the Son upholds 'all things by His powerful word', Hebrews 1:3. The correspondence is between the effectual word of God and a person who is that word. The type is exceeded because the Word became flesh, John 1:14, entering the world He made. The psalm has a God who speaks, and the Gospel has a God who speaks as a man.

typology.type: The waters gathered and commanded, verses 7 and 9
typology.fulfillment: The LORD gathers the sea and it stands at His command. In the Gospels, Jesus rises in the boat and rebukes the wind and the sea, and it becomes perfectly calm, Mark 4:39. The disciples ask, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?', Mark 4:41. The psalm has taught the reader to whom the sea belongs, and Psalm 107:29 has said that the LORD calms the storm to a whisper. The correspondence is between the God who commands the deep and a man who does the same. The type is exceeded by the identity revealed: the one who speaks to the storm is the one who spoke it into being.

typology.type: No king saved by his army, verses 16 and 17
typology.fulfillment: The psalm rejects the horse as a hope. Zechariah foresaw a king who would come 'righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey', and who would cut off the chariot and the war horse, Zechariah 9:9-10. Matthew shows Jesus entering Jerusalem in that manner, Matthew 21:5. Before Pilate He says, 'My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight', John 18:36, and in Gethsemane He declines the legions of angels, Matthew 26:53. The correspondence is between the psalm's theology of salvation and the shape of Christ's kingship. The type is exceeded because the king does not merely refuse the horse; He saves by giving His own life.

The call to sing a new song finds its final setting in the book of Revelation, where the four living creatures and elders sing, 'Worthy are You to take the scroll... because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation', Revelation 5:9. The song of the psalm, prompted by the word and work of God in creation, becomes a song prompted by redemption. The type is exceeded in its scope, since the new song is sung by people from every nation, and in its subject, since it praises the Lamb.

typology.type: The nation whose God is the LORD, verse 12
typology.fulfillment: Israel was the people chosen as God's inheritance. Peter says of the church, 'you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession', 1 Peter 2:9, and adds that those who were not a people are now the people of God, 1 Peter 2:10. The correspondence is the covenant blessing extended to all who belong to Christ. The type is exceeded in that the people are drawn from every nation and are made one in Christ, not by descent.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the word through which everything was made. John begins his Gospel by echoing Genesis 1, and he says that the Word was with God and was God, and that all things were made through Him, John 1:1-3. Paul repeats the claim: in Christ 'all things were created', and 'in Him all things hold together', Colossians 1:16-17, and Hebrews says He upholds all things by His powerful word, Hebrews 1:3. The psalm says, 'He spoke, and it came to be', and the New Testament says who was speaking. It is a careful claim. John does not say that the psalmist knew about the Son. He says that the God who spoke in Genesis and in the psalm spoke through His Son, and that the Son is that speech in person. The last book of the Bible names the rider on the white horse 'The Word of God', Revelation 19:13, and it is fitting that the one who was a word from the beginning should be so named at the end.

The second link is the authority over the sea. Verse 7 says that God gathers the waters, and verse 9 says that what He commands stands firm. When Jesus stills the storm with a word, Mark 4:39, the disciples do not ask what technique He used. They ask who He is. The answer that the psalm invites is that He is the one who commands the waters. Psalm 107:29 adds that it is the LORD who calms the storm to a whisper. In the Gospels, these acts of the LORD are done by Jesus in the open, and the people who see it are terrified because they see the identity behind the act.

The third link is the king who is not saved by his army. Zechariah saw a coming king riding a donkey, cutting off the chariot and the war horse and proclaiming peace to the nations, Zechariah 9:9-10, and Matthew quotes the first part of that prophecy at the entry into Jerusalem, Matthew 21:5. Jesus told Pilate that His kingdom was not of this world or His servants would fight, John 18:36, and He told Peter that He could call more than twelve legions of angels, Matthew 26:53. The psalm's claim that no warrior is delivered by great strength is realised in the king who conquered by being weak, and who was delivered from death not by force but by the power of God.

The fourth link is the new song. In Revelation the singing is around the throne, and its content is the Lamb who was slain and who purchased people from every nation, Revelation 5:9. The psalm's call to a fresh song is given its full occasion here.

There is a warning to keep. The psalm's word of the LORD is God's speech, and the Old Testament does not present it as a second person. The Christian claim is a reading made in the light of the incarnation, and it should not be made to sound as though the psalmist already taught the doctrine. What we can say is that the New Testament sees the psalm's God, whose word makes and sustains everything, revealed in Jesus, and that the psalm's trust in the counsel that stands forever finds its anchor in Him, who is the same yesterday, today and forever, Hebrews 13:8.
study.god:
The psalm gives a rich picture of God's character, and it begins with His word. The word of the LORD is 'upright', and His work is 'trustworthy', verse 4. The two go together: what He says is straight, and what He does is dependable, and there is no gap between His speech and His action. This is why the creation account is told the way it is. He spoke, and it came to be, and He commanded, and it stood firm. The God of the psalm is one whose speech is effective without any effort, and whose words can be relied on.

He is a God of both power and moral character. Verse 5 says He loves righteousness and justice, and that the earth is full of His loving devotion. The same God who piles up the seas loves justice. The psalm will not divide His might from His goodness, and so it invites reverence without terror. Verse 8 asks the whole earth to fear and revere Him, and verse 5 has just told the earth that it is full of His kindness. Awe and gladness come together.

He is sovereign over history. The plans of the nations are frustrated, and His counsel stands. The verbs are active, and God is not an observer. Yet the psalm does not describe a God who is far away. The same LORD who looks down from heaven in verse 13 shapes and considers the hearts of all in verse 15. His attention reaches from the rise and fall of empires to the workings of a single heart.

He is faithful to those who trust Him. The eyes of the LORD are on those who fear Him and hope in His loving devotion, verse 18, and the purpose of His watching is deliverance from death and provision in famine, verse 19. God is called 'our help and our shield', verse 20. The picture is of a God who is a defender in the very places where human strength fails.

He is also one who invites a response of joy and hope. The psalm does not end with a doctrine but with a prayer: 'May Your loving devotion rest on us, O LORD, as we put our hope in You.' It shows a people who know that they cannot make God's mercy come by their own action, and who ask for it while they wait.

For worship, the psalm teaches that praise should be skilful and joyful, that it should rest on the truth about God, and that it should bring trust in place of fear. Where a congregation is tempted to place its confidence in strength, numbers or clever plans, this psalm gives words for a different kind of security. It also sets the greatness of God and His personal care side by side: the One who made the stars by a word is the One whose eye is on those who fear Him.

crossReferences.note: The previous psalm ends by saying that loving devotion surrounds the one who trusts the LORD, and calls the righteous to rejoice. Psalm 33 opens with the same summons, using almost the same words, and then explains why rejoicing is right. Reading them together, the forgiven person of the first becomes the singing congregation of the second.

God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light. The psalm's 'He spoke, and it came to be' is a compact reading of this chapter. It shows that Israel treated creation by the word as the foundation of its worship, and that the psalm's teaching about God's word is anchored in the first page of the Bible.

At the blast of God's nostrils the waters piled up like a wall. The verb and the picture match verse 7, so the psalm uses the language of the exodus to speak of creation. It shows that Israel saw one God at work in the making of the world and in the deliverance of the people.

No wisdom, understanding or counsel can prevail against the LORD, and a horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory belongs to the LORD. It states the teaching of verses 10 and 16 to 17 in proverb form, and it shows that the psalm's theology was part of Israel's everyday wisdom.

Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who rely on horses and do not look to the Holy One of Israel. The prophet applies the truth of verse 17 to a real political choice, and shows what it meant in practice to prefer the horse to the LORD.

God declares the end from the beginning and says that His purpose will stand and all His good pleasure will be accomplished. It is the prophetic counterpart to verse 11, and it shows that the doctrine of the enduring counsel was a matter of God's own self declaration, not only of the psalmist's confidence.

By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God's command. The verse takes the psalm's teaching on creation and makes it an article of faith: the origin of the world is grasped by trusting God's word rather than by observing the process. It links belief in creation with the life of faith.

The Word was with God and was God, and through Him all things were made. John reads the creating speech of Genesis 1 and Psalm 33:6 as the act of the Word who became flesh. The passage is the New Testament's plainest statement of what the psalm's 'word of the LORD' is finally revealed to be.

All things were created through and for Christ, and in Him all things hold together. Paul moves from creation to sustaining, which fits the psalm's picture of a word that both makes and holds the world firm. It shows that the creating word of verse 6 continues its work in the present.

Jesus rebukes the wind and the sea, and they obey. The disciples' question, 'Who is this?', is the question the psalm has already answered about the LORD who commands the waters. The episode shows the psalm's God at work in Jesus, in the sight of frightened men in a boat.

A king comes humble and riding on a donkey, and God cuts off the chariot and the war horse. The prophet's picture of a king who does not depend on military means matches the psalm's teaching that no army saves a king. Matthew quotes the first verse at the entry into Jerusalem.

The elders sing a new song to the Lamb who was slain, who purchased people from every tribe and tongue and nation. The psalm's call to a new song has its answer here, in a song about redemption sung by a people gathered from all the earth.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a God who speaks, and this psalm is a meditation on that opening. 'God said' is the rhythm of Genesis 1, and the psalm turns it into a hymn: the heavens by His word, the stars by the breath of His mouth, the sea gathered as in a heap. It answers the questions of who made the world and by what power, and it answers them in a way that makes worship reasonable. What is true about the world is that a good God made it by His word.

The psalm also faces what went wrong. The nations plan and scheme, and their devices are the fruit of a world in which human beings have turned from God. Genesis 11 shows this in miniature at Babel, where a people made plans to make a name for themselves and were scattered. The psalm's claim that God frustrates the plans of the nations is the same thing seen from above. The tower is not built. The story of Israel then shows the same lesson: a small people is saved not by horses but by the LORD, at the sea, in the wilderness, and in the land, and it is warned again and again not to trust in chariots.

The middle of the story is the arrival of the Word. John writes the first sentence of his Gospel as a return to the first sentence of Genesis, and he says that the speech that made the world has taken flesh, John 1:14. The powerless king on a donkey is that Word, and the cross is where a kingdom without armies is established. In Him the plan of the LORD that stands forever is disclosed, and it is a plan that draws people from all nations to Himself, Ephesians 1:9-11. The verbs of the psalm, that He looks, considers, delivers and keeps alive, are given a face.

The story ends where the psalm's new song is sung. Revelation shows the redeemed singing to the Lamb, Revelation 5:9, and it shows the LORD dwelling with His people in a renewed creation, where death is gone and the hunger of verse 19 is no more, Revelation 7:16-17. The word that made the heavens makes all things new, Revelation 21:5. The prayer in the last verse, that God's loving devotion might rest on those who hope in Him, is answered in a world where hope has become sight. The psalm invites its readers to sing now, in the middle of the story, as those who know both how it began and how it will end.

sermon.title: The Counsel of the Lord Stands Forever
sermon.why: Piper preaches directly from Psalm 33:10-11, arguing that God's plans, not human corporate planning stripped of Him, must be the starting point for the church, since the counsel of the LORD alone stands forever.

quiz.q: What does the psalm say was made by the word of the LORD in verse 6?

options.text: The heavens and all the stars.
options.note: This verse celebrates creation itself as accomplished by God's spoken word and the breath of His mouth.

options.text: The sky's appearance only, without reference to the stars.
options.note: Close, since the sky is part of the picture, but the verse specifically names both the heavens and all the stars, not the sky's appearance alone.

options.text: The temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: The verse describes cosmic creation, not the construction of a specific building.

options.text: Nothing; the verse is purely metaphorical about human effort.
options.note: The verse makes a direct claim about the origin of the heavens and stars through God's word.

quiz.q: According to verses 10-11, what happens to the plans of the nations compared to the LORD's counsel?

options.text: The LORD frustrates the nations' plans, but His own counsel stands forever.
options.note: This is the direct contrast the psalm draws in these two verses.

options.text: The nations' plans sometimes succeed and sometimes fail, unpredictably.
options.note: Close, since human plans do vary in outcome, but the text makes a definite claim, that the LORD actively frustrates them while His own counsel stands forever, not mere unpredictability.

options.text: The nations' plans always succeed over God's purposes.
options.note: This is the reverse of what the text states.

options.text: The LORD has no involvement in the affairs of nations.
options.note: The text explicitly describes God's active frustration of national plans, not disengagement.

quiz.q: What does the psalm say about trusting in military strength in verses 16-17?

options.text: No king is saved by a vast army, and a horse is a vain hope for salvation.
options.note: These verses explicitly declare military strength insufficient for true deliverance.

options.text: A large army helps but ultimately cannot guarantee salvation on its own.
options.note: Close to the psalm's point, but understates it; the text states flatly that no king is saved by a vast army, not merely that an army alone is insufficient.

options.text: Horses are more reliable than any other resource.
options.note: The psalm specifically calls a horse a vain hope for salvation.

options.text: Kings should avoid having any army at all.
options.note: The point is not a prohibition on having an army, but a warning against trusting in it for salvation.

quiz.q: On whom are the eyes of the LORD, according to verse 18?

options.text: Those who fear Him and hope in His loving devotion.
options.note: This verse specifies the object of God's watchful, favorable attention.

options.text: All people equally, regardless of their relationship to Him.
options.note: Close, since God's general care extends broadly, but verse 18 specifically singles out those who fear Him and hope in His loving devotion for this attentive favor.

options.text: No one in particular; God is indifferent.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's claim about God's attentive care.

options.text: Only the priests serving in the temple.
options.note: The verse addresses those who fear the LORD generally, not a specific priestly office.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's final request in verse 22?

options.text: That God's loving devotion would rest on His people as they put their hope in Him.
options.note: This closing prayer ties the psalm's themes of God's character and human hope together.

options.text: That God would grant military victory immediately.
options.note: The closing request concerns loving devotion and hope, not a specific military request.

options.text: That God's help would come, without specific mention of His loving devotion.
options.note: Close, since help is implied by the request, but verse 22 specifically names God's loving devotion, chesed, as the object of the psalmist's hope, not generic help.

options.text: That the psalmist would be given more wealth.
options.note: The closing prayer concerns God's loving devotion and hope, not material gain.

questions: The psalm calls for a new song in response to God's works. What recent evidence of God's power or care in your life deserves a fresh song of praise rather than a routine one?
The psalm says the heavens were made by God's word alone. How does reflecting on the sheer power of God's spoken word change the size of the problem you are currently facing?

The psalm insists no king is saved by a vast army and no horse can guarantee victory. What modern equivalents, financial security, personal competence, or reputation, do you tend to trust the way ancient armies trusted horses?
God's eyes are on those who fear Him and hope in His loving devotion. Does your daily life reflect a settled hope in God's character, or do you find your hope shifting toward circumstances instead?

The psalm closes with a prayer that God's loving devotion would rest on His people as they hope in Him. Turn that same prayer into your own words today, what do you most need God's steadfast love to cover in your life right now?

translationNotes.note: A new song appears repeatedly across the Psalter and later in Revelation 5:9, always as a fresh response to a fresh display of God's saving work, not a replacement for older songs of praise.
He spoke, and it came to be echoes Genesis 1's repeated formula, 'And God said... and it was so,' underscoring creation by divine word alone, without struggle or opposition.

Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD reflects the unique covenant relationship of Israel, later extended in the New Testament to all who are in Christ, regardless of national origin, 1 Peter 2:9-10.
